51: This page opens Chapter 1: DESIRE—The Starting Point of All Achievement (The First Step to Riches). Hill returns to the Edwin C. Barnes story, noting that when Barnes climbed down from the freight train in Orange, N.J., he may have resembled a tramp, but his thoughts were those of a king. As he walked to Edison's office, his mind was at work—he saw himself standing in Edison's presence, asking for an opportunity to carry out the CONSUMING OBSESSION OF HIS LIFE: a BURNING DESIRE to become Edison's business associate. Hill emphasizes Barnes' desire was not a hope or wish but a keen, pulsating DESIRE that transcended everything else, and it was DEFINITE. The desire had been Barnes' dominating desire for a long time, beginning perhaps as a wish but becoming far more by the time he appeared before Edison. Years later, Barnes stood before Edison again—this time as his business partner. People who knew Barnes envied his 'break' but never investigated the cause of his success. Hill states Barnes succeeded because he chose a definite goal and placed all his energy, willpower, and effort behind it.
52: Hill explains Barnes did not become Edison's partner on day one. He was content to start at the most menial work as long as it provided one step toward his goal. Five years passed before the chance appeared—not one ray of hope or promise during all those years. To everyone else, he was just another cog in the Edison business wheel, but in his own mind HE WAS THE PARTNER OF EDISON EVERY MINUTE OF THE TIME. Hill calls this a remarkable illustration of the power of DEFINITE DESIRE. Barnes won because he wanted the association more than anything else, created a plan, and BURNED ALL BRIDGES BEHIND HIM. He did not say 'I will try to get a job' or 'I will work a few months and quit if no encouragement.' Instead he declared: 'I will start anywhere. I will do anything Edison tells me to do, but before I am through, I will be his associate.' He left no retreat: 'There is but ONE thing in this world that I am determined to have...I will burn all bridges behind me and stake my ENTIRE FUTURE on my ability to get what I want.' He had to win or perish. Hill then tells the story of a great warrior who burned his ships after sailing to enemy territory, telling his troops: 'We win—or we perish!' They won.
53: Hill draws the lesson: those who would win in any undertaking must be willing to burn their ships and cut all sources of retreat, maintaining a BURNING DESIRE TO WIN. He tells the story of the Great Chicago Fire of 1871: a group of merchants stood on State Street looking at smoking remains of their stores. All except one decided to leave Chicago. The one who stayed pointed at the remains and said, 'Gentlemen, on that very spot I will build the world's greatest store, no matter how many times it may burn down.' That merchant was Marshal Field, and the store was built—a towering monument to BURNING DESIRE. The easy thing would have been to do what fellow merchants did: pull up and go where going seemed easier. Hill says this is the same difference distinguishing Barnes from thousands of other Edison employees and practically all who succeed from those who fail. He then states that everyone who reaches the age of understanding money wishes for it, but wishing won't bring riches. Desiring riches with a state of mind that becomes an obsession, planning definite ways and means, and backing plans with persistence that doesn't recognize failure—that will bring riches. Hill then introduces the six definite, practical actions for transmuting DESIRE into financial equivalent. First: fix in your mind the exact amount of money you desire. Be definite—don't say 'I want plenty of money.'
54: Hill continues the six actions: Second—determine exactly what you intend to give in return for the money (there is no 'something for nothing'). Third—establish a definite date when you intend to possess the money. Fourth—create a definite plan for carrying out your desire and begin at once, ready or not. Fifth—write out a clear, concise statement of the amount, the time limit, what you intend to give in return, and the plan for accumulation. Sixth—read your written statement aloud twice daily, once before retiring and once after arising. AS YOU READ, SEE AND FEEL AND BELIEVE YOURSELF ALREADY IN POSSESSION OF THE MONEY. Hill stresses following all six actions, especially the sixth. He acknowledges the difficulty of 'seeing yourself in possession of money' before having it, but says a BURNING DESIRE will help. Only those who become 'money-conscious' ever accumulate great riches—meaning the mind is so saturated with DESIRE for money that one sees oneself already possessing it. The six actions came from Andrew Carnegie, who began as an ordinary laborer in steel mills and made these principles yield over $100 million. The actions were also approved by Thomas Edison as essential for any definite goal. They require no hard labor, sacrifice, or great education—but do require imagination to understand that money accumulation cannot be left to chance.
55: Hill states you can never have riches in great quantities UNLESS you work yourself into a white heat of DESIRE and actually BELIEVE you will possess them. He notes every great leader from civilization's dawn was a dreamer—Christianity became one of the greatest powers because its founder was an intense dreamer with vision to see realities in mental and spiritual form before physical transmutation. 'If you do not see great riches in your imagination, you will never see them in your bank balance.' Hill declares there has never been a greater opportunity for practical dreamers than now, as economic hardship has put people back at square one for a new race with huge stakes. The changed world favors those who had little opportunity under recent conditions when fear paralyzed growth. The world demands new ideas, new ways of doing things, new leaders, inventions, methods of teaching, marketing, books, literature, entertainment. Behind all this demand, the one quality needed is DEFINITENESS OF PURPOSE—knowledge of what one wants and a burning DESIRE to possess it. Practical dreamers have always been the pattern makers of civilization, harnessing unseen forces of unborn opportunity and converting them into skyscrapers, cities, factories, airplanes, and every convenience that makes life pleasant.
56: Hill emphasizes that tolerance and open mind are practical necessities for today's dreamer. Those afraid of new ideas are doomed before they start. There is no 'Wild West' to conquer but a vast business, financial, and industrial world to be remolded. He urges readers not to scorn the dreamer, to catch the spirit of great pioneers whose dreams gave civilization all its value—the burning desire to develop and market talents in a free land. He provides historical examples: Columbus dreamed of an Unknown World, staked his life, and discovered it. Copernicus dreamed of a multiplicity of worlds and revealed them—no one called him impractical after triumph; instead the world worshiped at his shrine, proving 'SUCCESS REQUIRES NO APOLOGIES, FAILURE PERMITS NO ALIBIS.' Hill states: if the thing you wish to do is right and you believe in it, go ahead and do it, never mind what 'they' say about temporary defeat, for 'they' perhaps do not know that EVERY FAILURE BRINGS WITH IT THE SEED OF AN EQUIVALENT SUCCESS.
57: Hill provides more examples of dreamers: Henry Ford, poor and uneducated, dreamed of a horseless carriage and put more wheels into operation than anyone who ever lived because he wasn't afraid to back his dreams. Thomas Edison dreamed of an electric lamp and despite more than 10,000 failures stood by his dream until it became physical reality—'Practical dreamers DO NOT QUIT!' Lincoln dreamed of freedom for slaves and nearly lived to see a united North and South translate his dream. The Wright brothers dreamed of a flying machine—evidence covers the world. Marconi dreamed of harnessing electromagnetic forces; his dream is evidenced in every radio and television set, making back-door neighbors of every nation. Interestingly, Marconi's 'friends' had him taken into custody and examined in a mental hospital when he announced he could send messages through the air without wires—but the dreamers of today fare better. The world has become accustomed to new discoveries and willing to reward the dreamer with new ideas. Hill quotes: 'The greatest achievement was at first and for a time a dream. The oak sleeps in the acorn; the bird waits in the egg; and in the highest vision of the soul a waking angel stirs. DREAMS ARE THE SEEDLINGS OF REALITIES.'
58: Hill calls dreamers to action: 'Awake, arise, and assert yourself!' Worldwide economic uncertainty has brought opportunity, teaching humility, tolerance, and open-mindedness. The world is filled with abundance of OPPORTUNITY the dreamers of the past never knew. A BURNING DESIRE TO BE, AND TO DO is the starting point; dreams are not born of indifference, laziness, or lack of ambition. He references the Tennessee Valley Authority dams as evidence of what a 'dreamer' President accomplished—something that once seemed like madness. Hill acknowledges readers may have suffered setbacks and defeat, feeling their heart crushed, but urges courage: these experiences have tempered their spiritual metal—they are assets of incomparable value. He notes all who succeed get off to a bad start and pass through heartbreaking struggles before arriving. The turning point usually comes at some crisis, through which they are introduced to their 'other selves.' Examples: John Bunyan wrote Pilgrim's Progress after imprisonment for religious views; O. Henry discovered his genius after misfortune and imprisonment in Columbus, Ohio—being forced through misfortune to become acquainted with his 'other self' and use his IMAGINATION, he discovered he was a great author instead of a criminal and outcast.
59: Hill continues with examples of those who discovered themselves through adversity: Edison started as a 'tramp' telegraph operator and failed innumerable times before discovering his genius. Charles Dickens began pasting labels on blacking pots; the tragedy of his first love penetrated his soul and converted him into a great author, producing first David Copperfield then a succession of works. Hill notes disappointment in love can drive many to drink and ruin because most never learn the art of transmuting emotions into constructive dreams—a power dealt with later as 'transmutation.' Helen Keller, deaf and blind from birth, proved no one is defeated until defeat is accepted as reality. Robert Burns, an illiterate, poverty-cursed drunkard, clothed beautiful thoughts in poetry. Booker T. Washington, born in slavery, handicapped by race and color, left his imprint on an entire nation through tolerance, open-mindedness, and dreaming. Beethoven was deaf, Milton was blind, yet their names will last as long as civilization because they dreamed and translated dreams into organized thought. Hill urges readers to kindle hope, faith, courage, and tolerance, promising that with these states of mind and knowledge of the principles, all else needed will come when READY. He distinguishes between WISHING for a thing and being READY to receive it—no one is ready until they BELIEVE they can acquire it.
60: Hill emphasizes the state of mind must be BELIEF, not mere hope or wish. Open-mindedness is essential for belief; closed minds don't inspire faith, courage, and belief. He makes a key point: no more effort is required to aim high in life, to demand abundance and prosperity, than to accept misery and poverty. He quotes Jessie B. Rittenhouse's poem 'My Wage': 'I bargained with Life for a penny, / And Life would pay no more... / For Life is a just employer, / He gives you what you ask... / I worked for a menial's hire / Only to learn, dismayed, / That any wage I had asked of Life, / Life would have willingly paid.' The poem illustrates that life gives what we demand of it. Hill then begins the story of 'Desire Outwits Mother Nature,' introducing his own son who was born without external physical signs of ears. The doctor admitted the child would likely be deaf and mute for life. Hill challenged this opinion silently—he was the child's father and decided his son would hear and speak. Nature could send a child without hearing organs but could not induce Hill to accept the reality of the affliction.
